lessonTitle: Documenting Injury, Preserving Evidence and Caring After Sexual Assault

blocks.text: Eighteen months after an emergency department visit, a barrister asks a registrar in the witness box to describe a bruise she recorded as 'bruise to arm'. No size, no site, no colour, no diagram. The registrar can say only what the note says. This unit teaches you to write a record that will still be useful when memory has faded and a court wants details.

blocks.markdown: A **medicolegal record** is a contemporaneous, factual account of what you saw and what you were told. It may be read by police, lawyers, courts and the patient. It should be accurate, legible, dated, timed and signed. It records **observation** (what is there), **history** (what the patient said, in quotation where possible) and, only if you are qualified and it is appropriate, a tentative **opinion** about consistency of findings with an account. It never states more certainty than the findings allow.

blocks.title: Contemporaneous record
blocks.text: A record made at the time of the examination or as soon afterwards as practicable, by the clinician who made the observations. Late additions are dated and labelled as late, and original entries are never altered or removed.

items: Site: use anatomical landmarks and distance from a fixed point, for example from the heel or the midline
Size: length and width in centimetres or millimetres using a ruler or calibrated scale; depth where relevant
Shape and pattern: linear, curved, patterned, with the orientation described
Colour and surface: record the colours, scabbing, swelling or tenderness without dating the injury precisely
Margins and edges: clean, irregular, abraded or bridged
Associated findings: swelling, bleeding, foreign material
Body diagram: mark each injury, number it and cross-reference to the written description
Photographs: with consent, include a scale and an identification label, a general view and close-ups

blocks.title: Recording a bruise correctly
blocks.prompt: A 33-year-old man attends with a bruise on the outer upper arm. A photograph is taken with a ruler beside it. On the photograph the ruler's 5.0 cm segment is 100 pixels long and the bruise measures 84 pixels across its longest axis.

steps.text: Establish the scale: 5.0 cm corresponds to 100 pixels, so 1 pixel corresponds to 0.05 cm.
Convert the bruise: 84 pixels multiplied by 0.05 cm per pixel gives 4.2 cm.
Record it as a measurement in the notes: 'bruise, approximately 4.2 cm in longest axis, outer aspect of upper arm, measured from photograph with scale and confirmed by ruler'.
Mark it on the body diagram, label it with a number, and describe colour and tenderness without stating that it is 'X days old'.

blocks.answer: The bruise is about 4.2 cm in its longest axis, recorded with site, colour, diagram and photograph.

rows: 3.5 cm by 1.2 cm, 4 cm above the elbow crease
Linear red-brown abrasion with a central scab
Patient states 'he pushed me against the door' (quoted)
Findings are consistent with the account but not specific
General view, close-up with scale and ID
blocks.caption: Language that records observation rather than conclusions.

blocks.markdown: **Preserving evidence.** Forensic evidence includes clothing, swabs, hair, fibres, fingernail samples, blood and urine, and the clinician's own records. Contamination and loss are the main threats. Use gloves, change them between samples, use separate labelled containers or tamper-evident bags, and package items according to the local forensic provider's guidance (for example, damp or biological items are not sealed in airtight plastic). Document what was collected, from where, by whom, at what time. Evidence should be collected only with valid consent unless the law or best interests framework applies.

**Chain of custody** is the documented record of every person who held an item from collection to court. It shows that the sample is what it claims to be and has not been changed. Each transfer is recorded with a signature, date and time. A gap or an unexplained transfer allows the defence to argue contamination or substitution, which may exclude the evidence.

blocks.title: Do not alter or discard
blocks.text: Never correct a record by overwriting. Cross out with a single line, add your initials and date, and add the correction. Never discard samples you are uncertain about; label them and ask the forensic provider or senior colleague. The aim of this unit is accurate documentation and lawful handling, not interpretation beyond your competence.

blocks.title: Maintaining chain of custody
blocks.prompt: A doctor takes a blood sample at 14:20 from a patient who has consented to forensic sampling after an assault. A police officer collects it at 16:45.

steps.text: At 14:20 label the tube with patient identifier, date, time, site and the doctor's name; place it in a tamper-evident bag and seal it.
Record in the notes and on the exhibit form: item, time, who collected it, where it is stored (for example a locked refrigerator), and who has access.
At 16:45, the officer and the doctor both sign and time the transfer form, noting that the seal is intact and the item number matches.
Keep a copy of the transfer record in the notes so the whole path from collection to police custody is documented.

blocks.answer: The item is traceable from collection to handover, with named people, times and an intact seal at each step.

blocks.markdown: **Care after sexual assault.** A person who discloses sexual assault needs safety, privacy, respect and medical care first. Care is delivered by trained clinicians, ideally in a sexual assault referral centre (SARC), and local arrangements vary. Medical needs include injury care, pregnancy risk, infection risk and mental health support; the clinician offers time-sensitive options and follows current guidance. Forensic examination is optional and separate from medical care. Consent is needed for **each** part: the examination, each type of sample, photography, and any sharing of information with police. The person can say no or stop at any point. Forensic windows for sample types differ and are set out in current guidance.

rows: Separate consent for each element; may be refused or withdrawn
Information sharing without consent only where there is a legal duty or serious risk to others
Consent must cover storage and use
Children or adults who lack capacity
Involve safeguarding leads; check current law and guidance
blocks.caption: Consent is specific, ongoing and revocable.

blocks.title: Confidentiality still applies
blocks.text: The patient's account and findings are confidential. Disclosure without consent is justified only in limited circumstances, such as a legal obligation or a serious risk of harm to others or a child. Before any disclosure, tell the patient what you plan to share and why where practicable, and record the decision and your reasons.

points: Medicolegal records are contemporaneous, factual, dated and signed, with measured, described and diagrammed injuries and clear separation of observation, history and opinion.
Evidence must be collected, packaged and labelled to avoid contamination, and a complete chain of custody shows each transfer with signature, date and time.
After sexual assault the patient's safety and medical needs come first, forensic examination is optional, and consent is needed for each step and can be withdrawn.
Confidentiality is maintained unless there is a legal duty or serious risk to others; document the reasons for any disclosure.

questions.stem: Which entry best documents a bruise for a medicolegal record?

options.text: Large bruise, probably from a punch, three days old
Bruise 4.0 cm by 2.5 cm, outer aspect of left thigh 12 cm above the knee crease, red-purple, tender, marked on body diagram and photographed with scale
Bruise on leg consistent with assault
Defensive bruise on the thigh

questions.correctOptionText: Bruise 4.0 cm by 2.5 cm, outer aspect of left thigh 12 cm above the knee crease, red-purple, tender, marked on body diagram and photographed with scale

distractorRationale.a: It gives no measurement, states mechanism and age with unwarranted certainty.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: it gives size, site relative to a landmark, colour and cross-references.
distractorRationale.c: It gives a conclusion not an observation.
distractorRationale.d: The label implies a conclusion about intent without justification.

questions.explanation: A good record gives measured size, a precise site from a landmark, a description and a cross-reference to diagram and photograph. It avoids terms that assert mechanism, age or intent beyond what the findings support.

questions.stem: In a photograph of a wound a scale shows that 3.0 cm corresponds to 60 pixels. The wound spans 150 pixels along its longest axis. What is its length in centimetres?
questions.explanation: Each pixel represents 3.0 divided by 60, which is 0.05 cm. Multiplying 150 pixels by 0.05 cm per pixel gives 7.5 cm. Wound measurements from photographs should be checked against a direct ruler measurement.

questions.stem: The colour of a bruise can be used to state its age precisely in days.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Bruise colour varies with depth, site, skin type and individual factors, so it is not a reliable clock. A record should describe colour rather than assert an exact age.

questions.stem: What best describes the purpose of a chain of custody record?

options.text: To prove that the sample came from the accused
To document each person who handled the item, with dates and times, to show that it was not altered or substituted
To record the patient's consent
To decide which laboratory tests are performed

questions.correctOptionText: To document each person who handled the item, with dates and times, to show that it was not altered or substituted

distractorRationale.a: It does not establish identity of a person responsible.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: it demonstrates continuity and integrity from collection to court.
distractorRationale.d: Test selection is a separate decision.

questions.explanation: Chain of custody shows continuity of possession. If a gap exists, the defence may argue contamination or substitution, which weakens or excludes the evidence.

questions.stem: A doctor removes a patient's clothing during a forensic examination. Which action best preserves evidence?

options.text: Combine all items in one bag to save space
Place each item separately in a labelled, sealed container according to local guidance, and record who handled it
Wash stained items before packaging
Discard items that look unimportant

questions.correctOptionText: Place each item separately in a labelled, sealed container according to local guidance, and record who handled it

distractorRationale.b: Correct: separate labelled sealed packaging with a record preserves integrity.
distractorRationale.d: Unimportant is a judgement that may be wrong.

questions.explanation: Separate packaging prevents transfer between items, and labelling and sealing with a record preserve integrity. The doctor documents the handling so each step can be explained.

questions.stem: Explain what is meant by chain of custody and why a gap in it matters to a court.
markingGuide: Defines it as the documented record of every person who held an item from collection to court
Mentions labelling, tamper-evident sealing and signed, dated, timed transfers
Explains that gaps allow the defence to suggest contamination or substitution
States that the court may give the evidence less weight or exclude it
Notes the clinician's role in making a contemporaneous record
questions.explanation: A complete chain shows the item is what it claims to be and unaltered. Gaps raise doubt and may reduce the evidence's weight.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman attends the emergency department 20 hours after a sexual assault and says she does not want the police involved. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Refuse to treat her until she agrees to report

Offer medical care and explain the options, including a forensic examination and referral to a specialist service, obtaining separate consent for each step and respecting her decision not to report, subject to legal exceptions
Contact the police immediately without telling her
Ask a relative to decide

questions.correctOptionText: Offer medical care and explain the options, including a forensic examination and referral to a specialist service, obtaining separate consent for each step and respecting her decision not to report, subject to legal exceptions

distractorRationale.a: Treatment must not be conditional on reporting.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: care and options are offered, consent is specific, and confidentiality respected.
distractorRationale.c: Disclosure without consent needs justification, such as a legal duty or serious risk to others.
distractorRationale.d: An adult with capacity decides for herself.

questions.explanation: A competent adult controls medical care, forensic sampling and police involvement. The clinician explains options, obtains consent for each element and maintains confidentiality unless an exception applies.

questions.stem: During a forensic examination after assault the patient asks to stop. What should the doctor do?

options.text: Finish the examination because samples are time-critical
Stop, check she is safe and comfortable, record the request and what was completed, and discuss options
Ask her partner to persuade her
Continue but reduce the extent

questions.correctOptionText: Stop, check she is safe and comfortable, record the request and what was completed, and discuss options

distractorRationale.a: Consent can be withdrawn at any time.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: respect withdrawal, ensure wellbeing and document.

questions.explanation: Consent is ongoing and revocable. The doctor stops, supports the patient and documents what was and was not done, so that the record is accurate.

questions.stem: A doctor may routinely give a competent adult patient's account of sexual assault to the police without her consent.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Confidentiality applies, and disclosure without consent is justified only in limited circumstances such as a legal duty or a serious risk to others or a child. Check current law and GMC guidance.

questions.stem: Outline the key principles in the care of a 24-year-old who discloses a sexual assault to you in a general practice setting, covering consent and confidentiality.
markingGuide: Prioritises safety, privacy, dignity and urgent medical needs
Explains that medical care, forensic examination, photography and police reporting are separate decisions, each needing the patient's consent
States that consent can be withdrawn at any time
Mentions referral to a specialist service such as a sexual assault referral centre, with current guidance on time-sensitive options
Describes confidentiality and the limited exceptions, with documentation of reasons
Mentions contemporaneous, factual records and, where relevant, safeguarding
questions.explanation: The patient leads the decisions. The clinician provides care, explains options, obtains specific consent and respects confidentiality, while documenting accurately.
